facts.fact: Name for the term: "Trùng huyết"
Name for the term: "Bloodworms"
Name for the term: "trùn huyết"
Name for the term: "Trùn huyết"
Bloodworms are the larvae of midges in the family Chironomidae; they are not true worms, since they have an exoskeleton and small clawed legs.
The red colour comes from a blood pigment (erythrocruorin) that helps the larvae survive in low-oxygen water.
The red colour of bloodworms is not caused by an artificial dye.
Chironomid larvae come in white, green, yellow and deep red; transparent ones are called glassworms.
Larvae grow to 10–25 mm, and the larval stage lasts from under 2 weeks to 7 weeks depending on temperature.
Bloodworm protein ranges from 47.7–62.5% of dry weight and fat from 4.9–28.6%; they are a good iron source.
A Vietnamese shop gives trùn huyết as 62,5% crude protein, 10,4% crude fat, 11,6% ash and 15,6% carbohydrate.
Nearly all fish eat bloodworms eagerly, and research links them as a supplement to better growth and spawning rates.
Frozen bloodworms have protein levels comparable to live tubificids, so they can substitute for them.
Bloodworms are sold in regular, jumbo and mini sizes.
Fresh live bloodworms have higher nutritional content but must be cleaned; frozen ones are more convenient, keep longer, are safer and easier to portion.
"Trùng Huyết Đông Lạnh" is sold in Vietnam as a blister pack of 24 cubes or a 200 g zip bag.
"Trùng Huyết Đông Lạnh - Thức Ăn Dinh Dưỡng Cho Cá Cảnh" is listed by a Vietnamese shop as a Vietnamese-made frozen product at 35.000đ.
"trùn huyết đen, trùn huyết đỏ, trùn huyết xanh" (black, red and green) are listed by a Vietnamese shop as kinds of trùn huyết by colour.
"Trùn huyết đông lạnh" is sold in Vietnam in blocks of several sizes at aquarium shops or ordered online.
"Trùng Huyết Đông Lạnh": thaw it first for small ornamental fish; large fish can be fed the cubes directly without thawing.
"Trùng Huyết Đông Lạnh": in tanks with large filters, switch the filter off while feeding or hold the food in a plastic funnel so the filter does not suck it up.
Frozen bloodworms can be dropped into the tank as a cube, which thaws quickly while fish eat.
A worm feeder cone releases frozen bloodworms slowly, slows fast eaters and keeps worms contained.
Frozen food can be thawed for a few minutes in a small jar of tank water, then fed with a pipette or turkey baster to reach fish that lose out at mealtime.
For picky eaters, frozen food can be thawed in a container without water with a few drops of vitamin supplement added.
Feed until the belly looks slightly rounded, and remove uneaten bloodworms after about 3–4 minutes.
A full frozen cube can be too much for one small fish; cut off a section or buy a slab that can be broken apart.
Live trùn huyết should be used right after buying or kept in the refrigerator, but not too cold, as that can kill them; do not keep them long in a bag or box.
Fresh bloodworms should be rinsed thoroughly before feeding to remove parasites.
Thaw only what will be used in one feeding, and buy only as much frozen bloodworm as will be used within about 6 months.
Leaving frozen food at room temperature for more than about 30 minutes lets bacteria grow and the food spoil.
Refreezing food that has thawed at room temperature is a mistake, as bacteria may have started growing.
Overfeeding bloodworms leaves uneaten food that fouls the water.
Overfeeding bloodworms can cause bloating.
Eating too much trùn huyết can cause digestive problems in fish.
Feeding only bloodworms can make fish 'addicted' and refuse other foods; mix in pellets and raise their share gradually, or fast fish 2 to 7 days.
Feeding frozen food alone can lead to long-term vitamin and nutrient deficiencies, especially when it is stored a long time.
Trùn huyết should be only one part of the diet, combined with dry and frozen foods.
Live trùn huyết showing signs of bacteria or mould should be thrown away, and leftovers discarded rather than reused.
Large imported frozen bloodworms have a chitinous exoskeleton and bristles that can block the stomach; some rainbowfish reportedly developed swollen abdomens and obstructions.
A veterinarian quoted by ANGFA warns against feeding larger bloodworms to discus, rainbowfish and some tetras.
Early fish fry lack chitinase to digest chitin; deaths were reported in 4–5 day old Clarias batrachus post-larvae fed late-stage bloodworm larvae and pupae.
Bloodworms are abundant in wastewater channels and sewage ponds, where health agencies sometimes spray insecticides.
Wild-collected chironomid larvae tested in Europe carried no zoonotic bacteria or tested amphibian pathogens, but lead was in excess in two samples and zinc low in four.
Researchers say chironomid larvae should not be the single diet item for amphibians because of possible nutritional imbalance and lead accumulation.
Bloodworm haemoglobins cause allergies in some people, mostly those who handle fish food: aquarists, fish farmers, fishermen and pet shop workers.
Reported bloodworm allergies in hobbyists include conjunctivitis, rhinitis with or without asthma, and urticaria.
Bloodworm dust is the worst exposure; freeze-dried bloodworms are anecdotally linked to more allergic reactions than frozen ones.
Allergic keepers can wear gloves and a face mask, use feeding tongs, and buy portioned frozen blocks that need no handling.
Amazonas Magazine says hand-washing is often considered ineffective against bloodworm allergy.
Captive breeding of bloodworms has largely failed because midges will not swarm and mate in captivity, though some cultivation succeeded in Southeast Asia.
